USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture heading into the October talks with China. Do not escalate to the planned 30% hike on List 3 (Oct 1) yet, but do not roll anything back. Use the October negotiations to test whether China's deepening economic pain translates into genuine concessions on structural issues (IP, tech transfer, enforcement). Maintain the Huawei entity-list pressure as a separate strategic lever.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The US holds meaningful leverage as of mid-September 2019. China's economy is deteriorating under tariff pressure: industrial production growth fell to 4.8% in July (worst in 17 years) and further to 4.4% in August, retail sales are slowing, and the yuan has breached 7/USD — prompting the US to designate China a currency manipulator. China has begun offering goodwill gestures (Sept 11-13 tariff exemptions on some US farm/industrial goods), signaling they want talks to succeed. Meanwhile, the US economy is under strain — manufacturing PMI hit its lowest since 2009 (50.3 in Aug), new export orders falling at the quickest pace in 10 years, and UBS warns of recession risk — but services remain in growth territory and unemployment is still historically low. The threat to US interests is real but asymmetric: China is hurting more. The risk of further escalation is that it tips the US itself into recession heading into an election year. The upcoming October talks (agreed Sept 5) are the 13th high-level round; after the Shanghai round produced nothing in July, patience is warranted but so is holding firm on existing leverage. Rolling back tariffs now would surrender the pressure that is finally producing Chinese concessions. Escalating further risks self-harm before talks even begin. The hold posture preserves optionality for both negotiation success and further escalation if talks fail.

sources_cited.excerpt: China announces first tariff-exemption list for some US products (16 categories; industrial inputs / chemicals / related — not a broad farm rollback).
Chinese state media reports soybeans, pork, and some other farm goods will be excluded from additional retaliatory tariffs (goodwill signal ahead of talks).
China and US agree to meet in October for trade negotiations. Deputy-level meetings in mid-September to prepare.
China's industrial production increased by just 4.4% in August compared to a year earlier. That's worse than the sector's performance in July, when it grew by 4.8%, its weakest growth in 17 years.

The August PMI indicates that US manufacturers are enduring a torrid summer, with the main survey gauge down to its lowest since the depths of the financial crisis in 2009. New export orders fall at quickest pace for 10 years.

The move clearly shows that 25% is not a ceiling on tariffs and thus must increase materially the uncertainty about the outlook for the trade war for businesses. Imports of goods have fallen 40% because of tariffs.
American tariffs on foreign goods had already climbed higher than any time since the 1960s. Average tariffs on Chinese imports to 21.2 percent, up from only 3.1 percent.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the current de-escalation posture — maintain recent goodwill gestures (tariff exemptions, farm-good exclusions) and engage constructively in the planned early-October talks in Washington. Do not make major structural concessions yet, but signal willingness to increase purchases of US agricultural and energy goods as a confidence-building measure. Avoid retaliatory escalation that would invite further US tariff hikes or entity-list additions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of 0.6 reflects serious but not yet existential economic pressure. Industrial output hit a 17.5-year low of 4.4% in August (Reuters, Sept 16), GDP growth fell to 6.2% in Q2 — a 27-year low (NYT, July 14) — and manufacturing PMI remains in contraction territory. The September 1 implementation of List 4A at 15% on ~$110-125B of additional Chinese imports, combined with the Huawei Entity List placement (May 16), means the trade war now covers virtually all bilateral exports and threatens China's tech self-sufficiency goals. The yuan's breach of 7/USD (Aug 5) and 11.5-year lows add FX pressure, though the IMF confirmed the rate is 'in line with fundamentals' (Aug 30).

However, China retains significant buffers: forex reserves rose unexpectedly to $3.107T in August (Reuters/SCMP, Sept 7), capital outflows remain controlled, and the PBOC has room for further RRR and rate cuts. The economy is slowing but not collapsing — this is manageable pain, not a crisis.

The action score of 0.15 (within the negotiate band) reflects a posture of engaged restraint. China's recent gestures — exempting 16 US product categories from tariffs (Sept 11) and excluding soybeans/pork from retaliation (Sept 13) — are correctly calibrated as small olive branches ahead of October talks. Retaliation would be counterproductive: it risks further US escalation (List 4B at 15% in December, more entity-list designations) and China's export sector cannot afford additional tariff coverage. The US economy is also showing strain (manufacturing employment down in battleground states per NPR, Sept 11), which gives Beijing some leverage — but only if talks proceed. Full concessions on structural issues (IP, tech transfer, state subsidies) would undermine CCP legitimacy and long-term strategic goals; these should be held in reserve as negotiating leverage, not given away under pressure.

US economy also showing strain in manufacturing/battleground states — mutual leverage
